title: The darkest psalm (Psalm 88)
hook: a psalm that ends in darkness, and it's still in the Bible

segments.voice: Yesterday, Job again: God shows up and doesn't explain, and the explaining friends are rebuked. Your line was show up, don't explain. Who did you show up for? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-nine.

Open a Bible to Psalm 88, and read the last line first. "Lover and friend hast thou put far from me, and mine acquaintance into darkness." That's the end. No turn. No but I will trust in thee. No hallelujah tacked on at the bottom. The psalm stops in the dark, like a phone call cut off mid-sentence. And it isn't tucked away in a footnote. It sits right there in the songbook, among the psalms of praise, read and sung and copied along with the rest. Today: the darkest psalm.

Start at the top. The first line, in the King James Bible: "O LORD God of my salvation, I have cried day and night before thee." God of my salvation. Whoever prays this is in the dark, but is still talking to someone. That thread holds the whole psalm together. Then the middle. The singer feels close to the grave, counted among the dead, forgotten. And then a run of questions, thrown straight at God: "Shall thy wonders be known in the dark? and thy righteousness in the land of forgetfulness?" And: "LORD, why castest thou off my soul? why hidest thou thy face from me?" No answer comes inside the psalm. The questions just hang there. Then the ending. Other lament psalms turn near the end, as Psalm 13 does: but I have trusted, I will sing. This one doesn't. The heading names Heman the Ezrahite, and the psalm leaves darkness as the last word, lover and friend gone. So why is it in the Bible at all? Jewish and Christian communities kept it and prayed it with the rest of the psalms. Some readers say that's exactly the point: the Bible makes room for a prayer with no happy ending. Someone in long grief, in depression, awake in the small hours, can find their own words already here, already counted as prayer. Other readers notice that the psalm is itself a kind of faith. Their reasoning: you don't keep crying day and night to someone you think isn't there. For them, the cry is itself a kind of trust. That's today's line: even darkness can be prayed. Not fixed first. Not tidied. Prayed, as it is.

Here's the practice: pray without a happy ending. Settle, and breathe. Let something that's still dark come to mind: a loss not healed, a question not answered, a fear that hasn't left. Don't wrap it up. Don't add a silver lining. Just say it, silently, as it is, and let it end where it ends. If you pray, you can say it to God the way Psalm 88 does, even if the last word is darkness. If you don't, say it to the quiet. Then rest in the plain fact that it's been said. The bell holds the time.
The darkest psalm. Psalm 88, a prayer that ends in darkness, and was kept and prayed all the same.
Your line: even darkness can be prayed. Today, read Psalm 88 once, all the way to its last line, and don't hurry off to a happier psalm afterward. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Some Christians pray Psalm 88 in times of grief or depression, and churches that pray the psalms in order, in daily offices, say it along with the others; some pastors point people to it as permission to pray honestly in the dark.

Editor pass: 'lament psalms often turn' (an unsupported generalization) now points to Psalm 13 as the example; the heading's name is no longer stated as the author; varied the hospital image and the 'bring to mind' practice opener, both repeated across this run.

Audit (fresh reviewer): narrator had asserted 'nobody keeps crying to a God they've stopped believing is there; the cry is the trust' and told the listener what they feel; now attributed to those readers. Hook's odd 'scrap found in a cave' (a needless Dead Sea Scrolls echo) replaced.
